subject: SIG follow-up: VPC peering vs Private Endpoint — egress IPs and ephemeral port behavior

Subject: SIG follow-up: VPC peering vs Private Endpoint — egress IPs and ephemeral port behavior

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Helix's security team is finishing the SIG and has two outstanding network questions before we sign off:

1) Egress IPs: we need a stable, small set of egress IPs for allowlisting outbound traffic from Redwood's service to our telemetry and update endpoints. Can you confirm whether Redwood can provide static egress IPs for dedicated/private deployments and if they differ between VPC peering and PrivateLink/Private Endpoints?

2) Ephemeral ports / NAT behavior: our firewall team wants to understand how ephemeral source ports are handled across persistent connections and whether port translation will vary if we use cross-account VPC peering vs Private Endpoint. Any docs or short evidence we can attach to the SIG would be ideal.

We are on a tight timeline — would appreciate concrete answers and any config snippets we can put in our runbook.

Thanks,
Evan Lopez
Senior Cloud Security Engineer
Helix Therapeutics

Subject: Re: SIG follow-up: VPC peering vs Private Endpoint — egress IPs and ephemeral port behavior

Hi Evan — great questions, thanks for the clear ask. Short answers up front, details below and attached evidence.

- Yes, for Redwood Private (VPC peering or PrivateLink) we can provide a stable set of egress IPs for outbound calls originating from our serving plane. The set is small (CIDR-sized /32s per AZ) and we publish an egress file for customers.
- Behavior differs slightly between VPC peering and PrivateLink: peering preserves original source addressing within the VPC route table (NAT depends on your routing), whereas PrivateLink (interface endpoints) causes traffic to traverse a managed interface and our egress NAT pools are applied. For SIG purposes we can provide the documented egress list for your chosen deployment mode.

I've attached our network guidelines and a current egress IP CSV for your SOC/SIG evidence. Karthik is looping in a short snippet for the firewall/NAT behavior and an explanation of ephemeral port handling. Monica will coordinate sign-off and timeline.

Attachments: redwood_vpc_guidelines.pdf, egress_ip_list-20270613.csv

Cheers,

Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: SIG follow-up: VPC peering vs Private Endpoint — egress IPs and ephemeral port behavior

Evan — adding the technical details you can paste into your network runbook:

1) Egress IPs (Dedicated/Private)
- For Private (VPC peering): outbound SNAT is not performed by Redwood if customers accept routes into their VPC and our instances have no NAT gateway on your side. If customers want a stable egress IP seen by external parties, we recommend configuring a NAT gateway in your VPC with an Elastic IP and updating the route for the Redwood subnets to flow through it. If you prefer Redwood-managed egress, choose PrivateLink and we will advertise our egress IP pool for allowlisting.

2) PrivateLink vs Peering — practical differences
- Peering: traffic is L3 routed. Source IP is preserved inside your VPC; ephemeral port numbers are unchanged. If your firewall is stateful and logs connections by source IP:port, you'll see the original ephemeral ports.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): we terminate at the interface; connections to external services originate from Redwood's egress NAT pool. Ephemeral source ports will be NAT-translated and may be remapped by our pool.

3) Ephemeral port ranges and connection churn
- Redwood uses ephemeral source ports in the 32768-60999 range for NATed outbound connections when using our managed egress. Persistent keepalives reuse source ports per TCP session where possible, but when sessions are torn down and reestablished you will see new ephemeral ports. For high-throughput telemetry, we recommend allowing the full ephemeral range and ensuring your firewall tracks short-lived flows.

4) Example firewall rule snippets (AWS security groups / iptables comments)
- If you are using Peering + Customer NAT: allow outbound TCP/443 from customer-EIP to telemetry endpoint; allow inbound ephemeral return traffic (established).
- If you are using PrivateLink + Redwood egress: allow inbound traffic from Redwood egress IPs (see attached CSV) on destination ports your services require; ensure stateful firewall rules accept dynamic ephemeral source ports.

If helpful I can produce a minimal CloudFormation example that demonstrates routing the Redwood subnets through a customer NAT with an Elastic IP.

-karthik
Karthik Iyer | Network Reliability Lead, Redwood Inference
